items.prompt: Sort the materials into soluble and insoluble in water.
hints: A soluble material seems to disappear when you stir it into water.
An insoluble material can still be seen, or it settles at the bottom.
Think about stirring sugar into tea, then stirring sand into water.
items.explanation: Sugar, salt and instant coffee dissolve in water, so they are soluble. Sand, chalk, flour, iron filings and marbles do not dissolve, so they are insoluble.

items.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: the liquid that does the dissolving
the mixture made when a substance dissolves
hints: In salty water, the salt is one part and the water is another part.
Solution is the name for the whole mixture, not for one part of it.
Start with the word insoluble. The letters in- at the start often mean not.
items.explanation: In salty water, salt is the solute, water is the solvent and the salty water is the solution. A material that does not dissolve is insoluble.

items.prompt: Mira stirs sugar into warm water. The sugar seems to disappear. What has happened to it?

options.why: Melting needs heat to turn one solid into a liquid on its own. Sugar in water dissolves.
The sugar is still there. You can taste it, and you can get it back by evaporating the water.

options.text: It has broken into pieces too small to see, spread through the water.

options.why: The sugar does not change into water. It mixes with the water.

hints: If the water tastes sweet, the sugar must still be in it somewhere.
Think about the difference between melting and dissolving.
Cross out the choices that say the sugar is gone or has changed into something else.
items.explanation: The sugar has dissolved. It has broken up into particles too small to see, which spread out through the water, so the water tastes sweet.

items.prompt: Choose 2 ways to make sugar dissolve faster.

options.why: Bigger lumps dissolve more slowly. Smaller grains dissolve faster.
Sugar dissolves more slowly in cold water.

options.text: put a lid on the glass
options.why: A lid does not change how fast sugar dissolves.

hints: Think about how you make sugar dissolve in a cup of tea quickly.
Moving the water and heating the water both help the sugar to mix in.
Cross out the choices that would slow dissolving down or make no difference.
items.explanation: Stirring and using warmer water both make sugar dissolve faster. Crushing the sugar into smaller grains would help too.

items.prompt: Dewi dissolves 20 g of salt in 200 g of water. What is the mass of the salt solution?
hints: When salt dissolves, it is still there, even though you cannot see it.
Nothing is lost when a solid dissolves, so the masses add together.
Start by adding the mass of the water to the mass of the salt.
items.explanation: Dissolving does not destroy the salt, so its mass is still there. 200 g + 20 g = 220 g of salt solution.

solution.say: The salt dissolves, but it does not disappear. Its mass is still in the glass.
Add the mass of the water and the mass of the salt.

items.prompt: Ahmad times how long a spoonful of sugar takes to dissolve in water at different temperatures. What does the bar chart show?

figure.alt: Bar chart of time for sugar to dissolve: 120 seconds at 20 °C, 75 seconds at 40 °C, 45 seconds at 60 °C and 25 seconds at 80 °C.

options.text: The hotter the water, the slower the sugar dissolves.
options.why: The bars get shorter as the water gets hotter, so dissolving takes less time.

options.text: Sugar does not dissolve in cold water.
options.why: At 20 °C the sugar still dissolved. It just took longer.
The times are very different at each temperature.

options.text: The hotter the water, the faster the sugar dissolves.

hints: Each bar shows the time taken. A shorter bar means a shorter time.
Compare the bar for the coldest water with the bar for the hottest water.
Read the time at 20 °C and at 80 °C. Decide which is quicker.
items.explanation: The time to dissolve falls from 120 seconds at 20 °C to 25 seconds at 80 °C. So the hotter the water, the faster the sugar dissolves.

items.prompt: Which of these is dissolving, not melting?

options.text: butter turning to liquid in a hot pan
options.why: Heat turns the butter from a solid into a liquid on its own. That is melting.

options.text: coffee granules mixing into hot water
ice turning to water in the sun
options.why: That is melting. Only one material is involved.

options.text: chocolate going soft in your hand
options.why: Warmth from your hand melts the chocolate.

hints: Melting needs only one material and heat. Dissolving needs a solid and a liquid.
For each choice, count how many different materials are involved.
Look for the choice where a solid mixes into a different liquid.
items.explanation: Coffee granules dissolve when they mix into the water and spread through it. Butter, ice and chocolate melt because heat turns each one from a solid into a liquid on its own.

items.prompt: Arif keeps adding salt to a glass of water and stirring. Soon, salt stays at the bottom however long he stirs. Why?

options.text: The water cannot dissolve any more salt, so the solution is saturated.
The salt has turned into sand.
options.why: The salt is still salt. It stops dissolving because the water cannot hold any more.

options.text: Stirring has made the salt insoluble.
options.why: Stirring helps salt dissolve faster. It does not stop it dissolving.
The water is still in the glass. It simply cannot hold any more salt at this temperature.

hints: There is a limit to how much salt one glass of water can dissolve.
Think about what happens when you keep adding sugar to a small cup of tea.
Cross out the choices that say the salt or the water has changed into something else.
items.explanation: A glass of water can only dissolve a certain amount of salt. When no more will dissolve, the solution is saturated, and any extra salt stays at the bottom.

items.prompt: Ana says that sugar melts in tea. Is she right? Explain the difference between melting and dissolving, with an example of each.

criteria.label: Says that sugar dissolves in tea
Explains dissolving: a solid spreads through a liquid
Explains melting: heat turns one solid into a liquid
Gives a correct example of each

planning: What happens to sugar in tea?
What happens to ice in the sun?
How many materials are involved each time?
items.model: Ana is wrong, because sugar dissolves in tea. Dissolving happens when a solid breaks into tiny pieces that spread through a liquid, like salt in water. Melting happens when heat turns a solid into a liquid on its own, like ice turning into water in the sun.
hints: Think about whether the sugar needs the tea, or only heat, to change.
Melting needs heat and one material. Dissolving needs a solid and a liquid.
items.explanation: Sugar dissolves in tea because it spreads through the liquid as tiny pieces. Melting is a change from solid to liquid caused by heat, with only one material involved.

items.prompt: At 20 °C, 100 g of water can dissolve about 36 g of salt. How much salt can 250 g of water dissolve at 20 °C?
hints: The more water there is, the more salt it can dissolve.
250 g of water is two and a half lots of 100 g.
Find the salt for 200 g of water first, then the salt for the extra 50 g.
items.explanation: 250 g of water is 2.5 times 100 g, so it can dissolve 2.5 × 36 g = 90 g of salt. Any salt beyond this would stay undissolved.

solution.say: 100 g of water dissolves 36 g of salt, so 200 g of water dissolves twice as much.
50 g of water is half of 100 g, so it dissolves half of 36 g.

items.prompt: Mira stirs salt into water until the water is clear. In this mixture, which is the solvent?

options.why: The salt is the solid that dissolves, called the solute.
The salty water is the whole mixture, called the solution.
The spoon is not part of the mixture.

hints: The solvent is the liquid that does the dissolving.
Salt is a solid.
Find the liquid in the question.
items.explanation: Water is the solvent because it dissolves the salt. The salt is the solute and the mixture is the solution.

items.prompt: Salt dissolves in water, so we say that salt is ___ in water.
hints: Some materials dissolve and some do not.
The opposite word is insoluble.
The word starts with s.
items.explanation: A material that dissolves is soluble. A material that does not dissolve is insoluble.

items.prompt: The table shows how much of each solid dissolves in 100 mL of water in a test. How many more grams of sugar than salt dissolve?

head: Solid
Mass that dissolves in 100 mL of water (g)
figure.alt: Table of the mass that dissolves in 100 millilitres of water: sugar 200 grams, salt 36 grams, baking soda 9 grams, chalk 0 grams.

hints: Find the sugar row and the salt row.
You need the difference between the two amounts.
Subtract the salt mass from the sugar mass.
items.explanation: 200 - 36 = 164 g more sugar than salt dissolves.

items.prompt: Joko dissolves 40 g of sugar in 250 g of water. What is the mass of the sugar solution?
hints: Nothing is lost when a solid dissolves.
Think of the mass of water plus the mass of sugar.
Add the two masses.
items.explanation: 250 + 40 = 290 g. The mass of the solution equals the mass of the water plus the mass of the sugar.

items.prompt: Tom tests how water temperature affects how fast sugar dissolves. Choose 3 things he must keep the same.
hints: One thing is changed and one is measured.
The rest must stay the same.
Cross out the temperature and the time taken.
items.explanation: Temperature is the thing changed and time is measured. Water volume, sugar mass and stirring are kept the same.

items.prompt: Dewi times how long the same mass of sugar takes to dissolve in warm water. How many times as quickly does icing sugar dissolve as a sugar cube?

head: Type of sugar
Time to dissolve (s)
figure.alt: Table of dissolving times: sugar cube 120 seconds, granulated sugar 60 seconds, icing sugar 20 seconds.

hints: Compare the cube time with the icing sugar time.
Divide the longer time by the shorter time.
120 divided by 20.
items.explanation: 120 / 20 = 6, so icing sugar dissolves 6 times as quickly. Smaller pieces have more surface touching the water.

items.prompt: Sort the changes into dissolving and melting.

items.text: An ice lolly on a warm day

hints: Dissolving needs a liquid to dissolve in.
Melting is a solid turning to liquid when it gets warm.
Ask whether the solid mixes into a liquid or turns to liquid by itself.
items.explanation: Dissolving happens when a solid mixes into a liquid. Melting happens when a solid is heated and turns into a liquid.

items.prompt: Put the steps in order for a fair test of how fast sugar dissolves.
items: Measure 100 mL of water into a beaker and record its temperature
Add one spoon of sugar and start the timer
Stir the water and stop the timer when no grains are left
Repeat the test and record each time
hints: Prepare the water first.
The timer starts when the sugar goes in.
Repeating comes last.
items.explanation: Set up the water and record its temperature first, then add the sugar and time it. Repeating the test makes the results more reliable.

items.prompt: Wulan weighs a cup with 200 g of water and 15 g of sugar on top: 215 g. After stirring until the water is clear, the scale still shows 215 g. What does this show?

options.text: The sugar is still in the water, even though we cannot see it.

options.why: The mass of a solution is the water plus the sugar, so the sugar is still there.

options.text: The sugar disappeared and the scale is wrong.
options.why: The scale is working. The mass stayed the same because the sugar is still there.
If it were heavier, the scale would show more than 215 g.

hints: Compare the mass before and after.
If something disappears, the mass would drop.
Ask what the unchanged mass tells you about the sugar.
items.explanation: The mass did not change, so nothing was lost. The sugar broke into tiny pieces that spread through the water.

items.prompt: When sugar dissolves, its pieces become too ___ to see. You can get the sugar back by letting the water ___.
hints: The sugar is still in the water.
Think about what is left in a dish after the water dries up.
What happens to water in a warm, dry place?
items.explanation: Dissolved sugar is in tiny pieces. When the water evaporates, the sugar is left behind.

items.prompt: Which of these makes a solution?

options.text: Stirring salt into water until it is clear

options.why: Sand does not dissolve. It sinks to the bottom or makes the water cloudy.
Flour makes the water cloudy and settles. It does not dissolve.
Pebbles do not dissolve at all.

hints: A solution looks clear and the solid cannot be seen.
Which solid disappears into the water?
Think about which material is soluble.
items.explanation: Salt dissolves in water to make a clear solution. Sand, flour and pebbles are insoluble.

items.prompt: Amara puts the same spoon of sugar into a cup of water at 20 °C and a cup at 60 °C. Both are stirred the same. What will she see?

options.text: The sugar dissolves faster in the 20 °C water.
options.why: Warmer water usually dissolves a solid faster, not slower.

options.text: The sugar dissolves at the same speed in both cups.
options.why: Temperature changes how fast things dissolve.

options.text: The sugar dissolves faster in the 60 °C water.
The sugar does not dissolve in the 60 °C water.
options.why: Sugar dissolves in warm water, usually faster than in cold.

hints: Think about how you make a hot drink.
Does warm water make the sugar dissolve faster or slower?
Compare the two temperatures.
items.explanation: Warm water dissolves most solids faster than cold water.

items.prompt: Label the parts of this dissolving test.

figure.alt: A glass beaker half full of clear water. A spoon stands in the water. Small yellow crystals lie in two small heaps on the bottom of the beaker.

hints: Tap a label, then tap its number.
The solid on the bottom has not dissolved.
The beaker is the glass container.
items.explanation: The spoon stirs the water. Some sugar has not dissolved, so it lies at the bottom of the beaker.

items.prompt: Tap the sugar that has not dissolved.

figure.alt: A glass beaker half full of clear water. A spoon stands in the water. Small yellow crystals lie in two small heaps on the bottom of the beaker.

hints: Dissolved sugar cannot be seen.
Look for pieces you can see.
Look at the bottom of the beaker.
items.explanation: The yellow crystals at the bottom are sugar that has not dissolved. Dissolved sugar is too small to see.

items.prompt: Citra times how long salt takes to dissolve in water at 50 °C. One reading is odd. She ignores it and takes the mean of the rest. What is her mean time?

head: Test
Time to dissolve (s)
figure.alt: Table of dissolving times at 50 degrees: test 1 31 seconds, test 2 29 seconds, test 3 58 seconds, test 4 30 seconds.

hints: One reading is very different from the other three.
Leave out the odd reading.
Add the three similar readings and divide by 3.
items.explanation: The 58 s reading is an anomaly. The mean of 31, 29 and 30 is 90 / 3 = 30 s.

items.prompt: True or false: Sugar dissolves in water to make a solution.
hints: Can you see the sugar afterwards?
It mixes in.
Dissolved sugar is in solution.
items.explanation: The sugar spreads out into very tiny pieces that mix evenly with the water.

items.prompt: True or false: Sand dissolves in water if you stir it long enough.
hints: Does sand disappear?
What happens when you stop stirring?
Sand is insoluble.
items.explanation: Sand is insoluble, so it does not dissolve. It stays as grains and settles at the bottom.

items.prompt: True or false: Stirring helps a solid to dissolve faster.
hints: What does a spoon do?
Water gets moved around.
Stirring speeds it up.
items.explanation: Stirring moves the dissolved parts away from the solid, so fresh water touches it and it dissolves quicker.

items.prompt: True or false: The mass of a solution is less than the mass of the water and the sugar added.
hints: Is the sugar still there?
Mass cannot just vanish.
The masses add up.
items.explanation: The sugar is still in the solution, so the mass is the same as the sugar and water together. Dissolving does not make anything disappear.

items.prompt: The liquid that dissolves a solid is the ___.
hints: In sugar water, it is the water.
The solid is the solute.
It starts with solv.
items.explanation: The solvent is the liquid that dissolves the solid.

items.prompt: Sam stirred sugar into 100 ml of water at different temperatures until no more would dissolve. At 10 °C, 3 spoons dissolved. At 30 °C, 5 spoons. At 50 °C, 7 spoons. At 70 °C, 9 spoons.

parts.prompt: How many more spoons dissolved at 70 °C than at 10 °C?
What must be kept the same?

hints: Find 50 °C in the text.
9 take away 3.
Look at how the spoons change.
items.explanation: 7 spoons at 50 °C. 9 - 3 = 6. Warmer water dissolves more. The volume of water stays the same.
